Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 75, verses 1–4:

The interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nay, I swear by the Day of Resurrection (1) and I swear by the self-reproaching soul (2). Does man think that We will not assemble his bones? (3) Yes, [We are] able to put together even his fingertips (4).﴾

The readers differed over the recitation of His saying: ﴿Nay, I swear by the Day of Resurrection.﴾ The majority of the readers of the major cities recited ﴿Lā uqsimu﴾ with [lā] [[The hadith 138 was mentioned earlier in abridged form, with this chain 137. We have elaborated on it there.]] separated from uqsimu, except al-Hasan and al-A'raj, for it is reported of them that they used to recite it ﴿La-uqsimu bi-yawmi al-qiyamah﴾, meaning: "I swear by the Day of Resurrection," and then the oath particle lam was prefixed to it.

The recitation that I do not permit other than in this place is "lā" separated, and uqsimu beginning a new clause, in accordance with what the readers of the major cities have, due to the consensus of the authoritative readers upon it.

Those who recited in the manner we have chosen differed in its interpretation. Some said that "lā" is superfluous (ṣilah), and the meaning of the statement is: "I swear by the Day of Resurrection."

Mention of those who said that:

- Abu Hisham al-Rifa'i related to us, saying: Ibn Yaman related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Ibn Juraij, from al-Hasan ibn Muslim ibn Yanaq, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding ﴿Lā uqsimu bi-yawmi al-qiyamah﴾, he said: "I swear by the Day of Resurrection."

- Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Mihran related to us, from Sufyan, from Ibn Juraij, from al-Hasan ibn Muslim, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, ﴿Lā uqsimu﴾, he said: "I swear."

Others among them said: Rather, "lā" entered as an emphasis of the statement.

Mention of those who said that:

I heard Abu Hisham al-Rifa'i say: I heard Abu Bakr ibn Ayyash say: His saying ﴿Lā uqsimu﴾ is an emphasis of the oath, like the saying "lā wallāhi" ("No, by God"). Some grammarians of Kufa said: "lā" is a rejection of a statement that had already been made by the polytheists who denied Paradise and Hellfire; then the oath is begun, so it was said: "I swear by the Day of Resurrection." He used to say: every oath that is preceded by something is a rejection of a statement, so "lā" must be placed before it, to distinguish thereby between the oath that is a denial and the oath that is a new beginning. He would say: Do you not see that you say, beginning, "By God, the Messenger is truly [right]"; but if you say, "No, by God, the Messenger is truly [right]," it is as if you had denied a people who had rejected it.

They also differed over whether this is an oath or not. Some said: It is an oath, in which our Lord swore by the Day of Resurrection and by the self-reproaching soul.

Mention of those who said that:

- Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Jarir related to us, from Mughirah, from Abu al-Khayr ibn Tamim, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said to me: "Where are you from?" I said: "From the people of Iraq." He said: "Which of them?" I said: "From the Banu Asad." He said: "From their ḥuraybi [[The verse is by al-Qaṭṭāmī, his Diwan: 41, and it occurs in the commentary on a verse of Surah Yusuf 12 (vol. 12, p. 94, Bulaq). He says it to Zufar ibn al-Harith al-Kilabi, whom he had captured in war, pardoned, gave him a hundred camels, and returned his property to him. He says: "Shall I disbelieve in what you have entrusted to me, when I have been given what I have been given?" Al-'aṭā' means "the giving," and therefore "the hundred" is put in the accusative by it. Al-ruta' is the plural of rāti', meaning camels grazing in a lush pasture, going and coming.]]? Or from those on whom God has bestowed favour?" I said: "No, rather from those on whom God has bestowed favour." He said to me: "Ask." I said: "Lā uqsimu bi-yawmi al-qiyamah." He said: "Your Lord swears by whatever He wills of His creation."

- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿Lā uqsimu bi-yawmi al-qiyamati wa-lā uqsimu bi-l-nafsi al-lawwamah﴾, he said: "He swears by both of them together."

Others said: Rather, He swears by the Day of Resurrection, and He did not swear by the self-reproaching soul. They said: the meaning of His saying ﴿and I swear by the self-reproaching soul﴾ is: "And I do not swear by the self-reproaching soul."

Mention of those who said that:

- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, who said: al-Hasan said: "He swears by the Day of Resurrection, and He did not swear by the self-reproaching soul."

The most correct of these opinions in my view is the view of the one who said: God swears by the Day of Resurrection and by the self-reproaching soul, and "lā" is a rejection of a statement that had preceded from a people, and a response to them.

We have said that this is the most correct of the opinions because what is known of people's speech in their discourse is that when one of them says, "No, by God, I did not do such-and-such," he intends by "lā" the rejection of a statement, and by "by God" the beginning of an oath; and likewise their saying, "I do not swear by God, I did not do such-and-such." Since what is known of the meaning of that is what we have described, it is necessary that all that comes of its like should proceed in the same manner, unless something of that departs from what is known by something that requires submission. Moreover: all the authoritative scholars agree that His saying ﴿Lā uqsimu bi-yawmi al-qiyamah﴾ is an oath; so likewise His saying ﴿wa-lā uqsimu bi-l-nafsi al-lawwamah﴾, unless some proof comes indicating that one of them is an oath and the other a report. We have shown that the recitation of one who reads the first word as ﴿la-uqsimu﴾ by joining the lam to uqsimu is an impermissible recitation, contrary to what the authoritative consensus holds. So the meaning of the statement is: "No, it is not as you say, O people, that God does not raise His servants alive after their death. I swear by the Day of Resurrection." And a group used to say: the resurrection of every soul is its death.

Mention of those who said that:

- Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Waki' related to us, from Sufyan and Mis'ar, from Ziyad ibn 'Ilaqah, from al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah, who said: "They say: 'The resurrection, the resurrection,' but the resurrection of each of them is his death."

- He said: Waki' related to us, from Mis'ar and Sufyan, from Abu Qubays, who said: "I attended a funeral in which 'Alqamah was present, and when he was buried he said: 'As for this one, his resurrection has taken place.'"

* *

And His saying: ﴿wa-lā uqsimu bi-l-nafsi al-lawwamah﴾

The people of interpretation differed over the interpretation of His saying ﴿al-lawwamah﴾. Some said: its meaning is: "And I swear by the soul that blames [itself] for good and evil."

Mention of those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Mu'ammal related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Ibn Juraij, from al-Hasan ibn Muslim, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding His saying ﴿wa-lā uqsimu bi-l-nafsi al-lawwamah﴾, he said: "It blames [itself] for good and evil."

- Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Waki' related to us, from Isra'il, from Simak, from Ikrimah, regarding ﴿wa-lā uqsimu bi-l-nafsi al-lawwamah﴾, he said: "It blames [itself] for good and evil."

- Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Jarir related to us, from Mughirah, from Abu al-Khayr ibn Tamim, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: I said to Ibn 'Abbas, "﴿wa-lā uqsimu bi-l-nafsi al-lawwamah﴾," and he said: "It is the blameworthy soul (al-nafs al-la'um)."

Others said: Rather, the meaning of that is that it blames itself for what has passed and regrets it.

Mention of those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us, and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿bi-l-nafsi al-lawwamah﴾, he said: "It regrets what has passed and blames itself for it."

Others said: Rather, al-lawwamah means: the wicked (al-fajirah).

Mention of those who said that:

- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, ﴿wa-lā uqsimu bi-l-nafsi al-lawwamah﴾, i.e., "the wicked."

Others said: Rather, it is the blameworthy (al-madhmumah).

Mention of those who said that:

- 'Ali related to me, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿wa-lā uqsimu bi-l-nafsi al-lawwamah﴾, he said: "The blameworthy."

These sayings we have mentioned from those from whom we have related them, although the wording of their speakers differs, are close in meaning; and the saying most consistent with the apparent sense of the revelation is that it blames its owner for good and evil and regrets what has passed. All the readers agree on reciting it with the separation of "lā" from uqsimu.

* *

And His saying: ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Does the son of Adam suppose that We will not be able to gather his bones after they have been scattered? Yes, We are able to do something greater than that: that We put together his fingertips (bananahu), which are the fingers of his hands and feet, and make them one thing like the hoof of a camel or the hoof of a donkey; so he would not take what he eats except with his mouth, like the rest of the beasts. But He separated the fingers of his hands, with which he takes, grasps, and closes and opens as he wills, and so made his form good.

Those of the people of interpretation said likewise to what we have said.

Mention of those who said that:

- Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Jarir related to us, from Mughirah, from Abu al-Khayr ibn Tamim, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said to me: "Ask." I said: ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones? Yes, [We are] able to put together even his fingertips.﴾ He said: "If He willed, He would make it a hoof or a hoof-like form."

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿Yes, [We are] able to put together his fingertips﴾, he said: "I am able to make his palm a hard pad like the hoof of a camel."

- Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Ibn 'Atiyyah related to us, from Isra'il, from Mughirah, from one who related to him from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿able to put together his fingertips﴾, he said: "We make it a hoof or a hoof-like form."

- He said: Waki' related to us, from al-Nadr, from Ikrimah, regarding ﴿to put together his fingertips﴾, he said: "To make it like the hoof of a camel or the hoof of a donkey."

- Ya'qub related to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayyah related to us, from Abu Raja', from al-Hasan, regarding His saying ﴿Yes, [We are] able to put together his fingertips﴾, he said: "He made it a hand, and made fingers which he closes and opens; and if He willed, He would have gathered them, so you would have had to protect the earth with your mouth; but He made you in good form." Abu Raja' said: Ikrimah was asked and said: "If He willed, He would have made it like the hoof of a camel."

- Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us, and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿to put together his fingertips﴾, he said: "His feet, like the hoof of a camel, so that he does nothing with them."

- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿Yes, [We are] able to put together his fingertips﴾: "By God, He is able to make his fingertips like the hoof of an animal or the hoof of a camel; and if He willed, He would have made it so; for he would then clean his food with his mouth."

- Ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿to put together his fingertips﴾, he said: "If He willed, He would make his fingertips like the hoof of a camel or the hoof of an animal."

- It was related to me from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd related to us, who said: I heard al-Dahhak say, regarding His saying ﴿to put together his fingertips﴾: "The banan are the fingers; He says: We are able to make his fingertips like the hoof of a camel."

The grammarians differed over the grammatical reason for the accusative of ﴿qadirin﴾. Some said: it is in the accusative because it stands in the place of nafʿal (we do); when it was turned into the active participle form, it took the accusative. They said the meaning of the statement is: "Does man suppose that We will not assemble his bones? Yes, We are able to put together his fingertips"; then nuqdir was changed to qadirin. Some grammarians of Kufa said: it is in the accusative by departure (al-khurūj) from najma'; as if it were said in the speech: "Does he suppose that We will not be able over it? Rather, [We are] able over something stronger than you." He means: "Yes, We are able, empowered, over more than that." He said: the people's saying "Yes, we are able" — when you turn it into qadirin, the accusative is an error, because the verb does not take the accusative by changing it from yaf'alu to fa'il. Do you not see that you say, "Are you standing up to us?" If you change it into the active participle you say, "Qa'im?", and it would be an error to say qa'iman; he said: They used to argue by the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"Upon me is an oath that I will never revile anyone in the world,
nor let come out of my mouth a false word."

They said: he intended "I do not revile, nor does [a word] come out," and when he changed it to "coming out" he put it in the accusative; and it was in the accusative because he intended: "I have vowed to my Lord not to revile anyone, nor to let a false word come out of my mouth"; and his saying "lā ashtumu" (I do not revile) is in the accusative position. Some grammarians of Basra said: it is in the accusative by [the verb] najma'u, i.e., "Rather, We gather them, able to put together his fingertips." This second saying is closer to correctness according to the school of the people of Arabic grammar.

Others said: Rather, the meaning of that is that it blames itself for what has passed and regrets it.

Mention of those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us, and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿bi-l-nafsi al-lawwamah﴾, he said: "It regrets what has passed and blames itself for it."

Others said: Rather, al-lawwamah means: the wicked (al-fajirah).

Mention of those who said that:

- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, ﴿wa-lā uqsimu bi-l-nafsi al-lawwamah﴾, i.e., "the wicked."

Others said: Rather, it is the blameworthy (al-madhmumah).

Mention of those who said that:

- 'Ali related to me, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿wa-lā uqsimu bi-l-nafsi al-lawwamah﴾, he said: "The blameworthy."

These sayings we have mentioned from those from whom we have related them, although the wording of their speakers differs, are close in meaning; and the saying most consistent with the apparent sense of the revelation is that it blames its owner for good and evil and regrets what has passed. All the readers agree on reciting it with the separation of "lā" from uqsimu.

* *

And His saying: ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Does the son of Adam suppose that We will not be able to gather his bones after they have been scattered? Yes, We are able to do something greater than that: that We put together his fingertips (bananahu), which are the fingers of his hands and feet, and make them one thing like the hoof of a camel or the hoof of a donkey; so he would not take what he eats except with his mouth, like the rest of the beasts. But He separated the fingers of his hands, with which he takes, grasps, and closes and opens as he wills, and so made his form good.

Those of the people of interpretation said likewise to what we have said.

Mention of those who said that:

- Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Jarir related to us, from Mughirah, from Abu al-Khayr ibn Tamim, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said to me: "Ask." I said: ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones? Yes, [We are] able to put together even his fingertips.﴾ He said: "If He willed, He would make it a hoof or a hoof-like form."

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿Yes, [We are] able to put together his fingertips﴾, he said: "I am able to make his palm a hard pad like the hoof of a camel."

- Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Ibn 'Atiyyah related to us, from Isra'il, from Mughirah, from one who related to him from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿able to put together his fingertips﴾, he said: "We make it a hoof or a hoof-like form."

- He said: Waki' related to us, from al-Nadr, from Ikrimah, regarding ﴿to put together his fingertips﴾, he said: "To make it like the hoof of a camel or the hoof of a donkey."

- Ya'qub related to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayyah related to us, from Abu Raja', from al-Hasan, regarding His saying ﴿Yes, [We are] able to put together his fingertips﴾, he said: "He made it a hand, and made fingers which he closes and opens; and if He willed, He would have gathered them, so you would have had to protect the earth with your mouth; but He made you in good form." Abu Raja' said: Ikrimah was asked and said: "If He willed, He would have made it like the hoof of a camel."

- Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us, and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿to put together his fingertips﴾, he said: "His feet, like the hoof of a camel, so that he does nothing with them."

- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿Yes, [We are] able to put together his fingertips﴾: "By God, He is able to make his fingertips like the hoof of an animal or the hoof of a camel; and if He willed, He would have made it so; for he would then clean his food with his mouth."

- Ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿to put together his fingertips﴾, he said: "If He willed, He would make his fingertips like the hoof of a camel or the hoof of an animal."

- It was related to me from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd related to us, who said: I heard al-Dahhak say, regarding His saying ﴿to put together his fingertips﴾: "The banan are the fingers; He says: We are able to make his fingertips like the hoof of a camel."

The grammarians differed over the grammatical reason for the accusative of ﴿qadirin﴾. Some said: it is in the accusative because it stands in the place of nafʿal (we do); when it was turned into the active participle form, it took the accusative. They said the meaning of the statement is: "Does man suppose that We will not assemble his bones? Yes, We are able to put together his fingertips"; then nuqdir was changed to qadirin. Some grammarians of Kufa said: it is in the accusative by departure (al-khurūj) from najma'; as if it were said in the speech: "Does he suppose that We will not be able over it? Rather, [We are] able over something stronger than you." He means: "Yes, We are able, empowered, over more than that." He said: the people's saying "Yes, we are able" — when you turn it into qadirin, the accusative is an error, because the verb does not take the accusative by changing it from yaf'alu to fa'il. Do you not see that you say, "Are you standing up to us?" If you change it into the active participle you say, "Qa'im?", and it would be an error to say qa'iman; he said: They used to argue by the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"Upon me is an oath that I will never revile anyone in the world,
nor let come out of my mouth a false word."

They said: he intended "I do not revile, nor does [a word] come out," and when he changed it to "coming out" he put it in the accusative; and it was in the accusative because he intended: "I have vowed to my Lord not to revile anyone, nor to let a false word come out of my mouth"; and his saying "lā ashtumu" (I do not revile) is in the accusative position. Some grammarians of Basra said: it is in the accusative by [the verb] najma'u, i.e., "Rather, We gather them, able to put together his fingertips." This second saying is closer to correctness according to the school of the people of Arabic grammar.

**Commentary on the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Nay, man wants to continue in sin ahead of himself (5). He asks, "When is the Day of Resurrection?" (6). So when the sight is dazzled (7), and the moon is eclipsed (8), and the sun and moon are joined together (9), man will say on that Day, "Where is the escape?" (10). No! There is no refuge (11). To your Lord on that Day is the place of rest (12).﴾**

Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Does the son of Adam not know that his Lord is able to gather his bones? Rather, he wants to press forward in disobedience to Allah, nothing turns him back from it, and he never repents of it, and he keeps postponing repentance.

The exegetes (ahl al-ta'wil) held views similar to what we have said.

Those who said this:

- Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Jarir related to us, from Mughirah, from Abu al-Khayr ibn Tamim al-Dabbi, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Nay, man wants to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾, he said: He presses forward.
- Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Nay, man wants to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾, he said: meaning hope (al-amal). Man says: I will act, then I will repent before the Day of Resurrection. It is also said: it is disbelief in the truth before the Resurrection.
- Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾, he said: He goes forward riding his head (i.e., headlong).
- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿Nay, man wants to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾, he said: al-Hasan said: You will not meet a son of Adam but his soul inclines towards disobedience to Allah, going forward, forward, except one whom Allah has protected.
- Ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from al-Hasan, regarding His saying: ﴿to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾, he said: Forward in sins.
- Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, from 'Amr, from Isma'il al-Suddi: ﴿Nay, man wants to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾, he said: Forward.
- Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Waki' related to us, from al-Nadr, from 'Ikrimah: ﴿Nay, man wants to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾, he said: Forward, not turning back from immorality.
- Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Waki' related to us, from his father, from Abu Ishaq, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: ﴿to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾, he said: "I will repent later."

Others said: Rather, the meaning is that he drives his head in pursuit of this world constantly, and does not remember death.

Those who said this:

- It was related to me from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd related to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His saying: ﴿Nay, man wants to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾: It is hope; man hopes: "I will live and obtain such-and-such from this world, and obtain such-and-such," and does not remember death.

Others said: Rather, the meaning is: Rather, man, meaning the disbeliever, wants to deny the Day of Resurrection.

Those who said this:

- 'Ali related to me, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Nay, man wants to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾, he said: The disbeliever denies the reckoning.
- Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying: ﴿Nay, man wants to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾: He denies what is ahead of him, the Day of Resurrection and the reckoning.

Others said: Rather, the meaning is: Rather, man wants to disbelieve in the truth before the Resurrection. According to this view, the pronoun in His saying ﴿amamahu﴾ (ahead of him) refers to the Resurrection, and we have already mentioned the report to that effect earlier.

* *

His saying: ﴿He asks, "When is the Day of Resurrection?"﴾

Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, says: The son of Adam, who constantly travels in disobedience to Allah, going forward, asks: When is the Day of Resurrection? (He asks) to postpone repentance. So Allah explains this to him, saying: ﴿So when the sight is dazzled, and the moon is eclipsed, and the sun and moon are joined together…﴾ to the end of the verse.

The exegetes held views similar to what we have said.

Those who said this:

- Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Ibn 'Atiyyah related to us, from Isra'il, from Abu Ishaq, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿He asks, "When is the Day of Resurrection?"﴾, he says: When is the Day of Resurrection? He said: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Whoever is asked about the Day of Resurrection, let him recite this surah.
- Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: ﴿He asks, "When is the Day of Resurrection?"﴾: When will that be? Then he recited: ﴿and the sun and moon are joined together﴾. He said: Thus it will be on the Day of Resurrection.

* *

And His saying: ﴿So when the sight is dazzled﴾

The readers (qurra') differed in reading this. Abu Ja'far al-Qari', Nafi' and Ibn Abi Ishaq read ﴿fa-idha baraqa﴾ with a fatha on the ra', meaning it became fixed (shakhas), and it is opened at death. Shaybah, Abu 'Amr and the majority of the readers of Kufa read ﴿bariqa﴾ with a kasra on the ra', meaning: it became frightened and split.

Ahmad ibn Yusuf related to me, saying: al-Qasim related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Harun, who said: I asked Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' about it, and he said: ﴿bariqa﴾ with a kasra means it became confused (haara). He said: I also asked 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Ishaq about it, and he said: ﴿baraqa﴾ with a fatha; it is only "baraqa" in the sense of the flash of fire and lightning. As for the sight, it is "baraqa" at death. He said: I informed Ibn Abi Ishaq of that, and he said: I took my reading from the shaykhs, Nasr ibn 'Asim and his companions. I mentioned this to Abu 'Amr, and he said: But I do not take from Nasr or his companions, as if he meant: I take from the people of the Hijaz.

Of the two readings, the more correct in our view is the kasra on the ra', ﴿fa-idha bariqa﴾, meaning: it became frightened and split, and it is opened from the terror of the Resurrection and the fright of death. Arab poetry also confirms this. Some transmitters recited to me from Abu 'Ubaydah al-Kilabi:

*When Ibn Subayh came to me, desiring,*
*I gave him a she-camel of 'Ays from my herd, and he was dazzled (faraqa / baraqa).*

[[By his saying "taṣdīrahā" he meant making them verbal nouns (maṣādir) from which verbal actions emanate, as in your saying: "dhahaba dhahāban" (he went a going); "dhahaba" emanated from your saying "dhahāb". It acts in this capacity as a verb. He meant that they bring out the verbal noun in the form of a noun so that it operates like it, as in your saying "al-kalām" is the noun of what you speak with; but they said: "kallamtuhu kalāman" (I spoke to him a speech), placing it in the position of "tikhlīm" (speaking to), and they derived from "kallama" a verbal noun in the form of the noun of what one speaks with, which is "al-kalām"; so the verbal noun was "kalāman".]]

And it was related to me from Abu Zakariyya al-Farra', who said: Some Arabs recited to me:

*Hanānah, who is in a long, sour mood, grieves me, / scratching dry shrubs of 'Ishraq.*
*So let yourself grieve, and do not grieve me, / treat the wounds and do not be dazzled.*

[[The report was mentioned earlier with its takhrij, number 137.]]

with a fatha on the ra' (baraqa). He explained it as meaning: do not be frightened by the severity of the wounds you have. He said: Likewise the sight is dazzled (yabruqu) on the Day of Resurrection.

The exegetes held views similar to what we have said.

Those who said this:

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿So when the sight is dazzled﴾, he said: By the dazzling of the sight is meant death, and the dazzling of the sight is the Hour.
- Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿baraqa al-basar﴾, he said: At death.
- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿So when the sight is dazzled﴾: the sight became fixed (shakhas).

* *

And His saying: ﴿and the moon is eclipsed﴾

He says: the light of the moon has gone.

The exegetes held views similar to what we have said.

Those who said this:

- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿and the moon is eclipsed﴾: its light has gone, so it has no light.
- Ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, from al-Hasan: ﴿and the moon is eclipsed﴾, it is its light; he says: its light has gone.

* *

And His saying: ﴿and the sun and moon are joined together﴾

Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, says: They are joined together in the going of light, so neither of them has any light. In the reading of 'Abd Allah, as was mentioned to me, it is ﴿wa-jumi'a bayna al-shamsi wal-qamar﴾ (and the sun and moon are joined). It was also said: they are gathered and then folded up, as His majestic praise says: ﴿When the sun is folded up﴾ (81:1). The reason it is said ﴿wa-jumi'a al-shamsu wal-qamar﴾ is what I have mentioned, that its meaning is that they were brought together. Some of the grammarians of Kufa said: It was said "wa-jumi'a" according to the usage of "wa-jumi'a al-nurān" (and the two lights were joined), as if it were said: "wa-jumi'a al-diyā'ān" (and the two lights were joined). This is the view of al-Kisa'i.

The exegetes held views similar to what we have said.

Those who said this:

- Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿and the sun and moon are joined together﴾, he said: They will be folded up on the Day of Resurrection.
- Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: ﴿and the sun and moon are joined together﴾: They are gathered, then thrown onto the earth.

* *

And His saying: ﴿When the sun is folded up﴾

He said: It is folded up on the earth, and the moon with it.

Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Sa'id ibn Abi Ayyub informed me, from Abu Shaybah al-Kufi, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from 'Ata' ibn Yasar, that he once recited this verse: ﴿and the sun and moon are joined together﴾, and said: They will be joined together on the Day of Resurrection, then they will be cast into the sea, and that will be the Great Fire of Allah.

* *

And His saying: ﴿He says, "On that Day man will say, 'Where is the escape?'"﴾

With a fatha on the fa' (al-mafarr). The readers of the cities recited it this way, because the 'ayn of the verb in this form (yafirru) is kasra. When the 'ayn of the form yaf'al is kasra, the Arabs open it in the verbal noun of the form maf'al when they speak it, so they say: "farra yafirru mafarran" (he fled, a fleeing), meaning "farran" (flight). As the poet said:

*O Bakr, rally for me Kulayb! / O Bakr, where, where is the flight!*

[[The word "yuwaddihu" is missing from the printed edition; in it instead of: "awwal kull..." it reads "fi kull..."]]

When this meaning is intended from the form maf'al, they say "ayna al-mafarr" with a fatha on the fa'. Likewise al-madabb, from "dabba yadubbu" (to creep), as one of them said:

*As if the remains of the trace upon its backs / are the creeping of ants upon the sand as it moves along.*

[[al-tadhkiya: slaughtering and cutting the throat. "Dhakkaytu al-shāh tadhkiyatan": I slaughtered the sheep.]]

It may be recited with a kasra on the dal, but the fatha is more common, and the Arabs also say it that way; it is a verbal noun with a kasra on the 'ayn. Al-Farra' claimed that both are dialects, and that it was heard: "jā'a 'alā madabb al-sayl" and "madibb al-sayl," and "mā fī qamīṣihi maṣahh" and "maṣihh." As for the Basrans, they open the 'ayn of maf'al in the verbal noun when the verb is of the form yaf'il, and they permit the kasra only when the maf'il is intended as the place one flees to, and likewise al-madrab: the place where one strikes, when the ra' is kasra. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he used to recite it with a kasra on the fa' and say: al-mafir is the place where the animal flees.

The reading I do not permit other than is the fatha on the fa' of al-mafarr, because the proof of the readers agrees on it, and because it is the well-known usage of the Arabs when flight is intended, and in this place it means flight. The meaning of the speech is: Man will say on the Day when he witnesses the terrors of the Day of Resurrection: Where is the escape from the horror of this which has descended, and there is no flight?

Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, says: ﴿Lā wazar﴾ (No refuge). His majestic praise says: There is no flight that benefits its doer, for his fleeing does not save him, nor is there anything to take refuge in, such as a fortress, a mountain, or a stronghold, from the command of Allah that has come, and that is the wazar.

The exegetes held views similar to what we have said.

Those who said this:

- 'Ali related to me, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Kallā lā wazar﴾, he says: No safeguard.
- Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Kallā lā wazar﴾, meaning: No fortress and no refuge.
- Ya'qub related to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayyah related to us, saying: Ibrahim ibn Tarif related to us, saying: I heard Mutarrif ibn al-Shikhkhir recite: ﴿Lā uqsimu bi-yawm al-qiyāmah﴾ (I swear by the Day of Resurrection), and when he came to ﴿Kallā lā wazar﴾ he said: It is the mountain. When people flee, they say: "'Alayka bil-wazar" (Upon you the refuge!).
- Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi related to us, from Shu'bah, from Adham, who said: I heard Mutarrif say: ﴿Kallā lā wazar﴾, he said: No, no mountain.
- Nasr ibn 'Ali al-Jahdami related to us, saying: My father related to me, from Khalid ibn Qays, from Qatadah, from al-Hasan, who said: ﴿Kallā lā wazar﴾, he said: No mountain.
- Ya'qub related to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayyah related to us, from Abu Raja', from al-Hasan, regarding His saying: ﴿Kallā lā wazar﴾, he said: The Arabs used to frighten one another. Two men would be with their livestock, and they would not notice anything until horsemen came to them, and one of them would say to his companion: "O so-and-so, the wazar, the wazar! The mountain, the mountain!"
- Abu Hafs al-Hayri related to me, saying: Mu'ammil related to us, saying: Abu Mawdud related to us, from al-Hasan, regarding His saying: ﴿Kallā lā wazar﴾, he said: No mountain.
- Muhammad ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Abu Mawdud, who said: I heard al-Hasan and he mentioned something similar.
- Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿lā wazar﴾, no refuge and no mountain.
- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah: ﴿Kallā lā wazar﴾, no mountain, no safeguard, no place of deliverance. Al-Hasan said: In the pre-Islamic period, the Arabs, when they feared an enemy, would say: "'Alaykum al-wazar," meaning: "Upon you the mountain!"
- Muhammad ibn 'Ubayd related to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak related to us, from Sufyan, from Sulayman al-Taymi, from Shabib, from Abu Qilabah regarding His saying: ﴿Kallā lā wazar﴾, he said: No fortress.
- Ahmad ibn Hisham related to us, saying: 'Ubayd Allah related to us, saying: Sufyan informed us, from Sulayman al-Taymi, from Shabib, from Abu Qilabah, the same.
- Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Mihran related to us, from Sufyan, from Sulayman al-Taymi, from Shabib, from Abu Qilabah, the same.

[[Abu Ja'far, may Allah be pleased with him, chose the best opinion for his argument. What he wrote before, and what comes after, is among the most sound of what has been said in explaining this place, over which minds and pens have stumbled. Clarifying what Abu Ja'far said: your saying "ism" in "bismi Allah" is in fact a verbal noun (ism masdar, or ism hadath), meaning that it is originally a name for the act of your naming a thing, like "al-kalām" as a name for the act of speaking (tkhlīm), and like "al-'aṭā'" as a name for the act of giving (i'ṭā'), and like "al-ghusl" as a name for the act of bathing (ightisāl). Its origin seems to be from your saying "sumtu al-shay' sumuwwan" (I named the thing, a naming), so they caused its triliteral verb to die out and its verbal noun "sumuw" remained; they dropped its final waw, so it became "sum," and they compensated for it with an alif at its beginning, so it became "ism," just as your saying "kalām" was from a triliteral verb "kalama kalāman" in the pattern of "dhahaba dhahāban"; they caused the triliteral verb to die out and its verbal noun "kalām" remained, and they made it a name for the act of speaking, then they derived the verbal noun of the quadriliteral form in the pattern of the name of this act, so they said "kallama yukallimu kalāman," meaning "kallama yukallimu takhlīman."]]

Thus they did likewise with their saying "sammā yusammī tasmiyah" (to name): they derived for this quadriliteral verb a verbal noun (maṣdar) on the pattern of the noun of the action, which is "ism" (name), and they said "sammā yusammī ismān," meaning "sammā yusammī tasmiyah." So your saying "kalām" in the sense of "takllīm" (speaking), and your saying "ism" in the sense of "tasmiyah," were both formed on the patterns of nouns of action. Accordingly, the word that is added to His name, exalted is He, in your saying "bismillāh" and similar expressions, is a verbal noun formed on the pattern of the noun of the action, namely "ism," from the quadriliteral verb "sammā yusammī," so it carries the meaning of its verbal noun, which is "tasmiyah." In this place and similar ones it means the verbal noun "tasmiyah," not the noun of the action of what one does by naming. (See: 123–124, al-Tabari's discussion under "ʾlh.")

And what Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari), may God have mercy on him, said is the most eloquent thing said in explaining this particle from Arabic speech. He examined it with great precision and subtlety, so much so that it was hidden from the great scholars who discussed the meaning of "ism" in "bismillāh" and similar expressions; they overlooked it because of its obscurity and the difficulty of its approach, and because of their familiarity with the discussion they had opened about "the name": whether it is the named (al-musammā) or other than it, whether it is an attribute of it, and what its definition and description are. That is a different chapter from the one we are in, so they mixed things up greatly. Then al-Tabari came and sifted out the truth with thorough sifting, and it is the most preponderant opinion in our view and the most deserving of precedence for whoever is granted understanding of it, as Abu Ja'far, may God forgive him, says. He will mention later evidence that will make the meaning even clearer and more manifest. Were it not for fear of prolixity, I would have brought the proofs for preferring al-Tabari's view, which they overlooked, over every opinion that preceded it or came after it.

Yahya ibn Wadih narrated to us, he said: Muslim ibn Tahman narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿No refuge (lā wazar)﴾ — he says: No fortress.

* Ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, he said: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah: ﴿No refuge﴾ — he said: No mountain.

* Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Waki' narrated to us, from his father, from a client of al-Hasan, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: ﴿No refuge﴾: No fortress.

* Waki' narrated to us, from Abu Hujayr, from al-Dahhak: No fortress.

* I was told by al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Ubayd narrated to us, he said: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His saying: ﴿Nay, no refuge (kallā lā wazar)﴾ — he means: the mountain, in the language of Himyar.

* Yunus narrated to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying: ﴿Nay, no refuge﴾ — he said: No place of hiding in which one may hide from that matter; no escape from it for him.

* *

And His saying: ﴿To your Lord on that Day is the place of rest (al-mustaqarr)﴾

The exalted One means: To your Lord, O human, on that day is the settling, which is He who causes all His creation to settle in their abode.

The interpreters of the Qur'an differed in its interpretation. Some of them said something similar to what we have said.

Those who said that:

* Yunus narrated to us, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying: ﴿To your Lord on that Day is the place of rest﴾ — he said: The people of Paradise settle in Paradise, and the people of the Fire in the Fire. And he recited the saying of God: ﴿And indeed the Abode of the Hereafter — that is the (true) life, if only they knew﴾.

Others said: What is meant by it is: To your Lord is the final end.

Those who said that:

* Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿To your Lord on that Day is the place of rest﴾: that is, the end.

**Commentary on the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Nay, man wants to continue in sin ahead of himself (5). He asks, "When is the Day of Resurrection?" (6). So when the sight is dazzled (7), and the moon is eclipsed (8), and the sun and moon are joined together (9), man will say on that Day, "Where is the escape?" (10). No! There is no refuge (11). To your Lord on that Day is the place of rest (12).﴾**

Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Does the son of Adam not know that his Lord is able to gather his bones? Rather, he wants to press forward in disobedience to Allah, nothing turns him back from it, and he never repents of it, and he keeps postponing repentance.

The exegetes (ahl al-ta'wil) held views similar to what we have said.

Those who said this:

- Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Jarir related to us, from Mughirah, from Abu al-Khayr ibn Tamim al-Dabbi, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Nay, man wants to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾, he said: He presses forward.
- Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Nay, man wants to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾, he said: meaning hope (al-amal). Man says: I will act, then I will repent before the Day of Resurrection. It is also said: it is disbelief in the truth before the Resurrection.
- Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾, he said: He goes forward riding his head (i.e., headlong).
- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿Nay, man wants to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾, he said: al-Hasan said: You will not meet a son of Adam but his soul inclines towards disobedience to Allah, going forward, forward, except one whom Allah has protected.
- Ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from al-Hasan, regarding His saying: ﴿to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾, he said: Forward in sins.
- Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, from 'Amr, from Isma'il al-Suddi: ﴿Nay, man wants to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾, he said: Forward.
- Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Waki' related to us, from al-Nadr, from 'Ikrimah: ﴿Nay, man wants to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾, he said: Forward, not turning back from immorality.
- Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Waki' related to us, from his father, from Abu Ishaq, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: ﴿to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾, he said: "I will repent later."

Others said: Rather, the meaning is that he drives his head in pursuit of this world constantly, and does not remember death.

Those who said this:

- It was related to me from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd related to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His saying: ﴿Nay, man wants to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾: It is hope; man hopes: "I will live and obtain such-and-such from this world, and obtain such-and-such," and does not remember death.

Others said: Rather, the meaning is: Rather, man, meaning the disbeliever, wants to deny the Day of Resurrection.

Those who said this:

- 'Ali related to me, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Nay, man wants to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾, he said: The disbeliever denies the reckoning.
- Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying: ﴿Nay, man wants to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾: He denies what is ahead of him, the Day of Resurrection and the reckoning.

Others said: Rather, the meaning is: Rather, man wants to disbelieve in the truth before the Resurrection. According to this view, the pronoun in His saying ﴿amamahu﴾ (ahead of him) refers to the Resurrection, and we have already mentioned the report to that effect earlier.

* *

His saying: ﴿He asks, "When is the Day of Resurrection?"﴾

Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, says: The son of Adam, who constantly travels in disobedience to Allah, going forward, asks: When is the Day of Resurrection? (He asks) to postpone repentance. So Allah explains this to him, saying: ﴿So when the sight is dazzled, and the moon is eclipsed, and the sun and moon are joined together…﴾ to the end of the verse.

The exegetes held views similar to what we have said.

Those who said this:

- Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Ibn 'Atiyyah related to us, from Isra'il, from Abu Ishaq, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿He asks, "When is the Day of Resurrection?"﴾, he says: When is the Day of Resurrection? He said: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Whoever is asked about the Day of Resurrection, let him recite this surah.
- Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: ﴿He asks, "When is the Day of Resurrection?"﴾: When will that be? Then he recited: ﴿and the sun and moon are joined together﴾. He said: Thus it will be on the Day of Resurrection.

* *

And His saying: ﴿So when the sight is dazzled﴾

The readers (qurra') differed in reading this. Abu Ja'far al-Qari', Nafi' and Ibn Abi Ishaq read ﴿fa-idha baraqa﴾ with a fatha on the ra', meaning it became fixed (shakhas), and it is opened at death. Shaybah, Abu 'Amr and the majority of the readers of Kufa read ﴿bariqa﴾ with a kasra on the ra', meaning: it became frightened and split.

Ahmad ibn Yusuf related to me, saying: al-Qasim related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Harun, who said: I asked Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' about it, and he said: ﴿bariqa﴾ with a kasra means it became confused (haara). He said: I also asked 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Ishaq about it, and he said: ﴿baraqa﴾ with a fatha; it is only "baraqa" in the sense of the flash of fire and lightning. As for the sight, it is "baraqa" at death. He said: I informed Ibn Abi Ishaq of that, and he said: I took my reading from the shaykhs, Nasr ibn 'Asim and his companions. I mentioned this to Abu 'Amr, and he said: But I do not take from Nasr or his companions, as if he meant: I take from the people of the Hijaz.

Of the two readings, the more correct in our view is the kasra on the ra', ﴿fa-idha bariqa﴾, meaning: it became frightened and split, and it is opened from the terror of the Resurrection and the fright of death. Arab poetry also confirms this. Some transmitters recited to me from Abu 'Ubaydah al-Kilabi:

*When Ibn Subayh came to me, desiring,*
*I gave him a she-camel of 'Ays from my herd, and he was dazzled (faraqa / baraqa).*

[[By his saying "taṣdīrahā" he meant making them verbal nouns (maṣādir) from which verbal actions emanate, as in your saying: "dhahaba dhahāban" (he went a going); "dhahaba" emanated from your saying "dhahāb". It acts in this capacity as a verb. He meant that they bring out the verbal noun in the form of a noun so that it operates like it, as in your saying "al-kalām" is the noun of what you speak with; but they said: "kallamtuhu kalāman" (I spoke to him a speech), placing it in the position of "tikhlīm" (speaking to), and they derived from "kallama" a verbal noun in the form of the noun of what one speaks with, which is "al-kalām"; so the verbal noun was "kalāman".]]

And it was related to me from Abu Zakariyya al-Farra', who said: Some Arabs recited to me:

*Hanānah, who is in a long, sour mood, grieves me, / scratching dry shrubs of 'Ishraq.*
*So let yourself grieve, and do not grieve me, / treat the wounds and do not be dazzled.*

[[The report was mentioned earlier with its takhrij, number 137.]]

with a fatha on the ra' (baraqa). He explained it as meaning: do not be frightened by the severity of the wounds you have. He said: Likewise the sight is dazzled (yabruqu) on the Day of Resurrection.

The exegetes held views similar to what we have said.

Those who said this:

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿So when the sight is dazzled﴾, he said: By the dazzling of the sight is meant death, and the dazzling of the sight is the Hour.
- Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿baraqa al-basar﴾, he said: At death.
- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿So when the sight is dazzled﴾: the sight became fixed (shakhas).

* *

And His saying: ﴿and the moon is eclipsed﴾

He says: the light of the moon has gone.

The exegetes held views similar to what we have said.

Those who said this:

- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿and the moon is eclipsed﴾: its light has gone, so it has no light.
- Ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, from al-Hasan: ﴿and the moon is eclipsed﴾, it is its light; he says: its light has gone.

* *

And His saying: ﴿and the sun and moon are joined together﴾

Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, says: They are joined together in the going of light, so neither of them has any light. In the reading of 'Abd Allah, as was mentioned to me, it is ﴿wa-jumi'a bayna al-shamsi wal-qamar﴾ (and the sun and moon are joined). It was also said: they are gathered and then folded up, as His majestic praise says: ﴿When the sun is folded up﴾ (81:1). The reason it is said ﴿wa-jumi'a al-shamsu wal-qamar﴾ is what I have mentioned, that its meaning is that they were brought together. Some of the grammarians of Kufa said: It was said "wa-jumi'a" according to the usage of "wa-jumi'a al-nurān" (and the two lights were joined), as if it were said: "wa-jumi'a al-diyā'ān" (and the two lights were joined). This is the view of al-Kisa'i.

The exegetes held views similar to what we have said.

Those who said this:

- Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿and the sun and moon are joined together﴾, he said: They will be folded up on the Day of Resurrection.
- Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: ﴿and the sun and moon are joined together﴾: They are gathered, then thrown onto the earth.

* *

And His saying: ﴿When the sun is folded up﴾

He said: It is folded up on the earth, and the moon with it.

Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Sa'id ibn Abi Ayyub informed me, from Abu Shaybah al-Kufi, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from 'Ata' ibn Yasar, that he once recited this verse: ﴿and the sun and moon are joined together﴾, and said: They will be joined together on the Day of Resurrection, then they will be cast into the sea, and that will be the Great Fire of Allah.

* *

And His saying: ﴿He says, "On that Day man will say, 'Where is the escape?'"﴾

With a fatha on the fa' (al-mafarr). The readers of the cities recited it this way, because the 'ayn of the verb in this form (yafirru) is kasra. When the 'ayn of the form yaf'al is kasra, the Arabs open it in the verbal noun of the form maf'al when they speak it, so they say: "farra yafirru mafarran" (he fled, a fleeing), meaning "farran" (flight). As the poet said:

*O Bakr, rally for me Kulayb! / O Bakr, where, where is the flight!*

[[The word "yuwaddihu" is missing from the printed edition; in it instead of: "awwal kull..." it reads "fi kull..."]]

When this meaning is intended from the form maf'al, they say "ayna al-mafarr" with a fatha on the fa'. Likewise al-madabb, from "dabba yadubbu" (to creep), as one of them said:

*As if the remains of the trace upon its backs / are the creeping of ants upon the sand as it moves along.*

[[al-tadhkiya: slaughtering and cutting the throat. "Dhakkaytu al-shāh tadhkiyatan": I slaughtered the sheep.]]

It may be recited with a kasra on the dal, but the fatha is more common, and the Arabs also say it that way; it is a verbal noun with a kasra on the 'ayn. Al-Farra' claimed that both are dialects, and that it was heard: "jā'a 'alā madabb al-sayl" and "madibb al-sayl," and "mā fī qamīṣihi maṣahh" and "maṣihh." As for the Basrans, they open the 'ayn of maf'al in the verbal noun when the verb is of the form yaf'il, and they permit the kasra only when the maf'il is intended as the place one flees to, and likewise al-madrab: the place where one strikes, when the ra' is kasra. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he used to recite it with a kasra on the fa' and say: al-mafir is the place where the animal flees.

The reading I do not permit other than is the fatha on the fa' of al-mafarr, because the proof of the readers agrees on it, and because it is the well-known usage of the Arabs when flight is intended, and in this place it means flight. The meaning of the speech is: Man will say on the Day when he witnesses the terrors of the Day of Resurrection: Where is the escape from the horror of this which has descended, and there is no flight?

Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, says: ﴿Lā wazar﴾ (No refuge). His majestic praise says: There is no flight that benefits its doer, for his fleeing does not save him, nor is there anything to take refuge in, such as a fortress, a mountain, or a stronghold, from the command of Allah that has come, and that is the wazar.

The exegetes held views similar to what we have said.

Those who said this:

- 'Ali related to me, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Kallā lā wazar﴾, he says: No safeguard.
- Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Kallā lā wazar﴾, meaning: No fortress and no refuge.
- Ya'qub related to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayyah related to us, saying: Ibrahim ibn Tarif related to us, saying: I heard Mutarrif ibn al-Shikhkhir recite: ﴿Lā uqsimu bi-yawm al-qiyāmah﴾ (I swear by the Day of Resurrection), and when he came to ﴿Kallā lā wazar﴾ he said: It is the mountain. When people flee, they say: "'Alayka bil-wazar" (Upon you the refuge!).
- Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi related to us, from Shu'bah, from Adham, who said: I heard Mutarrif say: ﴿Kallā lā wazar﴾, he said: No, no mountain.
- Nasr ibn 'Ali al-Jahdami related to us, saying: My father related to me, from Khalid ibn Qays, from Qatadah, from al-Hasan, who said: ﴿Kallā lā wazar﴾, he said: No mountain.
- Ya'qub related to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayyah related to us, from Abu Raja', from al-Hasan, regarding His saying: ﴿Kallā lā wazar﴾, he said: The Arabs used to frighten one another. Two men would be with their livestock, and they would not notice anything until horsemen came to them, and one of them would say to his companion: "O so-and-so, the wazar, the wazar! The mountain, the mountain!"
- Abu Hafs al-Hayri related to me, saying: Mu'ammil related to us, saying: Abu Mawdud related to us, from al-Hasan, regarding His saying: ﴿Kallā lā wazar﴾, he said: No mountain.
- Muhammad ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Abu Mawdud, who said: I heard al-Hasan and he mentioned something similar.
- Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿lā wazar﴾, no refuge and no mountain.
- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah: ﴿Kallā lā wazar﴾, no mountain, no safeguard, no place of deliverance. Al-Hasan said: In the pre-Islamic period, the Arabs, when they feared an enemy, would say: "'Alaykum al-wazar," meaning: "Upon you the mountain!"
- Muhammad ibn 'Ubayd related to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak related to us, from Sufyan, from Sulayman al-Taymi, from Shabib, from Abu Qilabah regarding His saying: ﴿Kallā lā wazar﴾, he said: No fortress.
- Ahmad ibn Hisham related to us, saying: 'Ubayd Allah related to us, saying: Sufyan informed us, from Sulayman al-Taymi, from Shabib, from Abu Qilabah, the same.
- Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Mihran related to us, from Sufyan, from Sulayman al-Taymi, from Shabib, from Abu Qilabah, the same.

[[Abu Ja'far, may Allah be pleased with him, chose the best opinion for his argument. What he wrote before, and what comes after, is among the most sound of what has been said in explaining this place, over which minds and pens have stumbled. Clarifying what Abu Ja'far said: your saying "ism" in "bismi Allah" is in fact a verbal noun (ism masdar, or ism hadath), meaning that it is originally a name for the act of your naming a thing, like "al-kalām" as a name for the act of speaking (tkhlīm), and like "al-'aṭā'" as a name for the act of giving (i'ṭā'), and like "al-ghusl" as a name for the act of bathing (ightisāl). Its origin seems to be from your saying "sumtu al-shay' sumuwwan" (I named the thing, a naming), so they caused its triliteral verb to die out and its verbal noun "sumuw" remained; they dropped its final waw, so it became "sum," and they compensated for it with an alif at its beginning, so it became "ism," just as your saying "kalām" was from a triliteral verb "kalama kalāman" in the pattern of "dhahaba dhahāban"; they caused the triliteral verb to die out and its verbal noun "kalām" remained, and they made it a name for the act of speaking, then they derived the verbal noun of the quadriliteral form in the pattern of the name of this act, so they said "kallama yukallimu kalāman," meaning "kallama yukallimu takhlīman."]]

Thus they did likewise with their saying "sammā yusammī tasmiyah" (to name): they derived for this quadriliteral verb a verbal noun (maṣdar) on the pattern of the noun of the action, which is "ism" (name), and they said "sammā yusammī ismān," meaning "sammā yusammī tasmiyah." So your saying "kalām" in the sense of "takllīm" (speaking), and your saying "ism" in the sense of "tasmiyah," were both formed on the patterns of nouns of action. Accordingly, the word that is added to His name, exalted is He, in your saying "bismillāh" and similar expressions, is a verbal noun formed on the pattern of the noun of the action, namely "ism," from the quadriliteral verb "sammā yusammī," so it carries the meaning of its verbal noun, which is "tasmiyah." In this place and similar ones it means the verbal noun "tasmiyah," not the noun of the action of what one does by naming. (See: 123–124, al-Tabari's discussion under "ʾlh.")

And what Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari), may God have mercy on him, said is the most eloquent thing said in explaining this particle from Arabic speech. He examined it with great precision and subtlety, so much so that it was hidden from the great scholars who discussed the meaning of "ism" in "bismillāh" and similar expressions; they overlooked it because of its obscurity and the difficulty of its approach, and because of their familiarity with the discussion they had opened about "the name": whether it is the named (al-musammā) or other than it, whether it is an attribute of it, and what its definition and description are. That is a different chapter from the one we are in, so they mixed things up greatly. Then al-Tabari came and sifted out the truth with thorough sifting, and it is the most preponderant opinion in our view and the most deserving of precedence for whoever is granted understanding of it, as Abu Ja'far, may God forgive him, says. He will mention later evidence that will make the meaning even clearer and more manifest. Were it not for fear of prolixity, I would have brought the proofs for preferring al-Tabari's view, which they overlooked, over every opinion that preceded it or came after it.

Yahya ibn Wadih narrated to us, he said: Muslim ibn Tahman narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿No refuge (lā wazar)﴾ — he says: No fortress.

* Ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, he said: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah: ﴿No refuge﴾ — he said: No mountain.

* Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Waki' narrated to us, from his father, from a client of al-Hasan, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: ﴿No refuge﴾: No fortress.

* Waki' narrated to us, from Abu Hujayr, from al-Dahhak: No fortress.

* I was told by al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Ubayd narrated to us, he said: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His saying: ﴿Nay, no refuge (kallā lā wazar)﴾ — he means: the mountain, in the language of Himyar.

* Yunus narrated to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying: ﴿Nay, no refuge﴾ — he said: No place of hiding in which one may hide from that matter; no escape from it for him.

* *

And His saying: ﴿To your Lord on that Day is the place of rest (al-mustaqarr)﴾

The exalted One means: To your Lord, O human, on that day is the settling, which is He who causes all His creation to settle in their abode.

The interpreters of the Qur'an differed in its interpretation. Some of them said something similar to what we have said.

Those who said that:

* Yunus narrated to us, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying: ﴿To your Lord on that Day is the place of rest﴾ — he said: The people of Paradise settle in Paradise, and the people of the Fire in the Fire. And he recited the saying of God: ﴿And indeed the Abode of the Hereafter — that is the (true) life, if only they knew﴾.

Others said: What is meant by it is: To your Lord is the final end.

Those who said that:

* Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿To your Lord on that Day is the place of rest﴾: that is, the end.

**Commentary on the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Nay, man wants to continue in sin ahead of himself (5). He asks, "When is the Day of Resurrection?" (6). So when the sight is dazzled (7), and the moon is eclipsed (8), and the sun and moon are joined together (9), man will say on that Day, "Where is the escape?" (10). No! There is no refuge (11). To your Lord on that Day is the place of rest (12).﴾**

Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Does the son of Adam not know that his Lord is able to gather his bones? Rather, he wants to press forward in disobedience to Allah, nothing turns him back from it, and he never repents of it, and he keeps postponing repentance.

The exegetes (ahl al-ta'wil) held views similar to what we have said.

Those who said this:

- Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Jarir related to us, from Mughirah, from Abu al-Khayr ibn Tamim al-Dabbi, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Nay, man wants to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾, he said: He presses forward.
- Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Nay, man wants to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾, he said: meaning hope (al-amal). Man says: I will act, then I will repent before the Day of Resurrection. It is also said: it is disbelief in the truth before the Resurrection.
- Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾, he said: He goes forward riding his head (i.e., headlong).
- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿Nay, man wants to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾, he said: al-Hasan said: You will not meet a son of Adam but his soul inclines towards disobedience to Allah, going forward, forward, except one whom Allah has protected.
- Ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from al-Hasan, regarding His saying: ﴿to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾, he said: Forward in sins.
- Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, from 'Amr, from Isma'il al-Suddi: ﴿Nay, man wants to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾, he said: Forward.
- Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Waki' related to us, from al-Nadr, from 'Ikrimah: ﴿Nay, man wants to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾, he said: Forward, not turning back from immorality.
- Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Waki' related to us, from his father, from Abu Ishaq, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: ﴿to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾, he said: "I will repent later."

Others said: Rather, the meaning is that he drives his head in pursuit of this world constantly, and does not remember death.

Those who said this:

- It was related to me from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd related to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His saying: ﴿Nay, man wants to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾: It is hope; man hopes: "I will live and obtain such-and-such from this world, and obtain such-and-such," and does not remember death.

Others said: Rather, the meaning is: Rather, man, meaning the disbeliever, wants to deny the Day of Resurrection.

Those who said this:

- 'Ali related to me, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Nay, man wants to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾, he said: The disbeliever denies the reckoning.
- Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying: ﴿Nay, man wants to continue in sin ahead of himself﴾: He denies what is ahead of him, the Day of Resurrection and the reckoning.

Others said: Rather, the meaning is: Rather, man wants to disbelieve in the truth before the Resurrection. According to this view, the pronoun in His saying ﴿amamahu﴾ (ahead of him) refers to the Resurrection, and we have already mentioned the report to that effect earlier.

* *

His saying: ﴿He asks, "When is the Day of Resurrection?"﴾

Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, says: The son of Adam, who constantly travels in disobedience to Allah, going forward, asks: When is the Day of Resurrection? (He asks) to postpone repentance. So Allah explains this to him, saying: ﴿So when the sight is dazzled, and the moon is eclipsed, and the sun and moon are joined together…﴾ to the end of the verse.

The exegetes held views similar to what we have said.

Those who said this:

- Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Ibn 'Atiyyah related to us, from Isra'il, from Abu Ishaq, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿He asks, "When is the Day of Resurrection?"﴾, he says: When is the Day of Resurrection? He said: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Whoever is asked about the Day of Resurrection, let him recite this surah.
- Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: ﴿He asks, "When is the Day of Resurrection?"﴾: When will that be? Then he recited: ﴿and the sun and moon are joined together﴾. He said: Thus it will be on the Day of Resurrection.

* *

And His saying: ﴿So when the sight is dazzled﴾

The readers (qurra') differed in reading this. Abu Ja'far al-Qari', Nafi' and Ibn Abi Ishaq read ﴿fa-idha baraqa﴾ with a fatha on the ra', meaning it became fixed (shakhas), and it is opened at death. Shaybah, Abu 'Amr and the majority of the readers of Kufa read ﴿bariqa﴾ with a kasra on the ra', meaning: it became frightened and split.

Ahmad ibn Yusuf related to me, saying: al-Qasim related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Harun, who said: I asked Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' about it, and he said: ﴿bariqa﴾ with a kasra means it became confused (haara). He said: I also asked 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Ishaq about it, and he said: ﴿baraqa﴾ with a fatha; it is only "baraqa" in the sense of the flash of fire and lightning. As for the sight, it is "baraqa" at death. He said: I informed Ibn Abi Ishaq of that, and he said: I took my reading from the shaykhs, Nasr ibn 'Asim and his companions. I mentioned this to Abu 'Amr, and he said: But I do not take from Nasr or his companions, as if he meant: I take from the people of the Hijaz.

Of the two readings, the more correct in our view is the kasra on the ra', ﴿fa-idha bariqa﴾, meaning: it became frightened and split, and it is opened from the terror of the Resurrection and the fright of death. Arab poetry also confirms this. Some transmitters recited to me from Abu 'Ubaydah al-Kilabi:

*When Ibn Subayh came to me, desiring,*
*I gave him a she-camel of 'Ays from my herd, and he was dazzled (faraqa / baraqa).*

[[By his saying "taṣdīrahā" he meant making them verbal nouns (maṣādir) from which verbal actions emanate, as in your saying: "dhahaba dhahāban" (he went a going); "dhahaba" emanated from your saying "dhahāb". It acts in this capacity as a verb. He meant that they bring out the verbal noun in the form of a noun so that it operates like it, as in your saying "al-kalām" is the noun of what you speak with; but they said: "kallamtuhu kalāman" (I spoke to him a speech), placing it in the position of "tikhlīm" (speaking to), and they derived from "kallama" a verbal noun in the form of the noun of what one speaks with, which is "al-kalām"; so the verbal noun was "kalāman".]]

And it was related to me from Abu Zakariyya al-Farra', who said: Some Arabs recited to me:

*Hanānah, who is in a long, sour mood, grieves me, / scratching dry shrubs of 'Ishraq.*
*So let yourself grieve, and do not grieve me, / treat the wounds and do not be dazzled.*

[[The report was mentioned earlier with its takhrij, number 137.]]

with a fatha on the ra' (baraqa). He explained it as meaning: do not be frightened by the severity of the wounds you have. He said: Likewise the sight is dazzled (yabruqu) on the Day of Resurrection.

The exegetes held views similar to what we have said.

Those who said this:

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿So when the sight is dazzled﴾, he said: By the dazzling of the sight is meant death, and the dazzling of the sight is the Hour.
- Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿baraqa al-basar﴾, he said: At death.
- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿So when the sight is dazzled﴾: the sight became fixed (shakhas).

* *

And His saying: ﴿and the moon is eclipsed﴾

He says: the light of the moon has gone.

The exegetes held views similar to what we have said.

Those who said this:

- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿and the moon is eclipsed﴾: its light has gone, so it has no light.
- Ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, from al-Hasan: ﴿and the moon is eclipsed﴾, it is its light; he says: its light has gone.

* *

And His saying: ﴿and the sun and moon are joined together﴾

Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, says: They are joined together in the going of light, so neither of them has any light. In the reading of 'Abd Allah, as was mentioned to me, it is ﴿wa-jumi'a bayna al-shamsi wal-qamar﴾ (and the sun and moon are joined). It was also said: they are gathered and then folded up, as His majestic praise says: ﴿When the sun is folded up﴾ (81:1). The reason it is said ﴿wa-jumi'a al-shamsu wal-qamar﴾ is what I have mentioned, that its meaning is that they were brought together. Some of the grammarians of Kufa said: It was said "wa-jumi'a" according to the usage of "wa-jumi'a al-nurān" (and the two lights were joined), as if it were said: "wa-jumi'a al-diyā'ān" (and the two lights were joined). This is the view of al-Kisa'i.

The exegetes held views similar to what we have said.

Those who said this:

- Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿and the sun and moon are joined together﴾, he said: They will be folded up on the Day of Resurrection.
- Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: ﴿and the sun and moon are joined together﴾: They are gathered, then thrown onto the earth.

* *

And His saying: ﴿When the sun is folded up﴾

He said: It is folded up on the earth, and the moon with it.

Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Sa'id ibn Abi Ayyub informed me, from Abu Shaybah al-Kufi, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from 'Ata' ibn Yasar, that he once recited this verse: ﴿and the sun and moon are joined together﴾, and said: They will be joined together on the Day of Resurrection, then they will be cast into the sea, and that will be the Great Fire of Allah.

* *

And His saying: ﴿He says, "On that Day man will say, 'Where is the escape?'"﴾

With a fatha on the fa' (al-mafarr). The readers of the cities recited it this way, because the 'ayn of the verb in this form (yafirru) is kasra. When the 'ayn of the form yaf'al is kasra, the Arabs open it in the verbal noun of the form maf'al when they speak it, so they say: "farra yafirru mafarran" (he fled, a fleeing), meaning "farran" (flight). As the poet said:

*O Bakr, rally for me Kulayb! / O Bakr, where, where is the flight!*

[[The word "yuwaddihu" is missing from the printed edition; in it instead of: "awwal kull..." it reads "fi kull..."]]

When this meaning is intended from the form maf'al, they say "ayna al-mafarr" with a fatha on the fa'. Likewise al-madabb, from "dabba yadubbu" (to creep), as one of them said:

*As if the remains of the trace upon its backs / are the creeping of ants upon the sand as it moves along.*

[[al-tadhkiya: slaughtering and cutting the throat. "Dhakkaytu al-shāh tadhkiyatan": I slaughtered the sheep.]]

It may be recited with a kasra on the dal, but the fatha is more common, and the Arabs also say it that way; it is a verbal noun with a kasra on the 'ayn. Al-Farra' claimed that both are dialects, and that it was heard: "jā'a 'alā madabb al-sayl" and "madibb al-sayl," and "mā fī qamīṣihi maṣahh" and "maṣihh." As for the Basrans, they open the 'ayn of maf'al in the verbal noun when the verb is of the form yaf'il, and they permit the kasra only when the maf'il is intended as the place one flees to, and likewise al-madrab: the place where one strikes, when the ra' is kasra. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he used to recite it with a kasra on the fa' and say: al-mafir is the place where the animal flees.
